newsitem.title: USA: Former soldier is a racist, not a killer - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Former soldier is a racist, not a killer - lawyer.

text.p: A prosecutor urged jurors Thursday to convict a white, former U.S. Army paratrooper of first-degree murder in the racially motivated shooting of a black couple even though he did not fire the fatal shots.
"If you run with the pack, you're responible for the kill," Prosecutor John Dickson said of murder defendant Malcolm Wright during closing arguments at Wright's trial.
Defence attorney Jonathan Broun acknowledged in his closing arguments that Wright was with triggerman James Burmeister when Burmeister shot and killed Jackie Burden and Michael James.
But he said Wright planned only to hunt black people to harass and beat up, and "did not shoot anybody and did not want anyone to die."
Broun said the decision to kill began and ended with Burmeister, who was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to two life terms for shooting the couple at point-blank range.
"Racism is disgusting, despicable and just plain wrong, but this is not a referendum on racism," Braun said. "Malcolm is a racist but he's not a murderer."

But Dickson told the jury of 11 whites and one black that Burmeister killed the couple because he wanted to earn a spider web tattoo like Wright's. The tattoo is a skinhead symbol signifying that the wearer has killed a black person. Both Burmeister and Wright were members of a skinhead group at the Army's Fort Bragg in North Carolina.

"It is only after Malcolm Wright comes into the picture that James Burmeister and Randy Meadows get involved in violent activity," said Dickson referring to the state's key witness, who testified at both Wright's and Burmeister's trials.
"What does this tell you about this defendant's motive, intent, premeditation and deliberation? There were two fingers on the trigger that night," Braun said.
Wright, 22, faces two counts of first-degree murder and one count of conspiracy to commit murder.
The jury deliberated briefly late on Thursday and adjourned without reaching a verdict. They will resume on Friday morning.

Prosecutors will seek the death penalty if Wright is convicted of first-degree murder. Judge Coy Brewer ruled jurors may find him guilty of a lesser charge of second-degree murder, which carries a maximum penalty of 20 years and five months in prison without parole for each count.
If convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to die, Wright could choose the gas chamber or lethal injection.

Meadows pleaded guilty to assault charges and was to be sentenced in the fall. In exchange for his testimony against Burmeister and Wright, prosecutors dropped two counts against him of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.
